content.title: About
content.content: Scallops are bivalve mollusks from the family Pectinidae. When steamed or boiled they retain a delicate sea flavor, a faint sweetness and a tender yet slightly firm texture. Scallops are commonly served as an appetizer, in salads, soups, or tossed with pasta.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scallops can filter up to 20 liters of water per hour, helping to keep their environment clean.
More than 300 species exist, but the blue mussel (Mytilus edulis) and the great scallop (Pecten maximus) are most widely consumed.
Scallops are capable of changing sex during their life cycle, often starting as males and later becoming females.
In ancient Rome, scallops were considered a delicacy and served at lavish banquets with wine.
Scallops grow quickly; they can increase their biomass five‑ to ten‑fold in a single year.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Scallops provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent source of complete animal protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: They contain less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, most of which are polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system health; scallops deliver over 100 % of the daily value in a 100‑g serving.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals aid immune function, metabolism, and skin health.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Scallops provide EPA and DHA, which are beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked scallops may harbor Vibrio bacteria that cause gastroenteritis. Always cook until shells fully open.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from hives to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Scallops contain about 50 mg of cholesterol per 100 g, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: In certain regions scallops can accumulate cadmium or lead; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam scallops for 5–7 minutes or boil for 3–4 minutes until the shells open. Serve with lemon, butter‑garlic sauce, or add to risotto, paella, and seafood salads. Discard any scallops whose shells do not open after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh raw scallops should be kept in the refrigerator (0–2 °C) in a sealed container covered with a damp cloth and used within 24 hours. Frozen scallops retain quality for up to 3 months; thaw them in the refrigerator before cooking.
